item.title: 'Lioness' star weighs in on what drove Taylor Sheridan's unexpected decision for her character
item.description: Elizaveta Neretin reacts to Taylor Sheridan's outcome for her "Lioness" character Oleksandra Balakin in the season 3 finale.
item.content:encoded:
WARNING: Spoilers below.

"Lioness" star Elizaveta Neretin reacted to Taylor Sheridan's bombshell season 3 finale, which saw her character, Oleksandra Balakin, killed off.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Neretin — who played the Ukrainian double agent — said she expected Oleksandra's fate. The character had been captured by American forces and recruited to help rescue Joe (Zoe Saldaña) after she was kidnapped.

In the episode, which aired Sunday night, Oleksandra was killed.

'LIONESS' SEASON 3 FINALE REVEALS WHO ORCHESTRATED JOE'S KIDNAPPING ALL ALONG

"I thought it was going to happen. So when he called, and he told me, I was like, 'Yeah, I get it.' I'm sad for Oleksandra and what Oleksandra represents, but I understand the choice. It does serve this. It serves to show how the whole system is. Like American or not American, the whole system and the people that work in the system. It's all sharks, you know, so it just demonstrates how people are," she told Fox News Digital.

Neretin said she would have preferred a different outcome for Oleksandra but understood why Sheridan made the decision.

"I would love a different ending for her, but like I said, I understand why it had to happen. But, of course, I would have a good ending for her. I just wonder if being a triple agent, I think your days are numbered. I don't think you can pull that off and live to an old age unless you give up on family you have, which I don't think she would."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"If you give up on the family you have, perhaps you could find a way to hide somewhere, you know what I mean? But the way she fights for her country, I think she cares way too much, way more about that outcome than her life. I think that she made that decision a long time ago," Neretin said.

The actress said she never asked Sheridan whether he had considered an alternative ending for Oleksandra. Instead, she trusted his creative judgment and did not try to challenge him while working on the series.

"No, I didn't challenge him. I just remember he shortened Oleksandra's name a certain way, and I just suggested, I was like, 'By the way, the short version of Oleksandra in Ukrainian is Alessa.' And he was like, 'Yeah, that works,'" she began. "I didn't challenge him, it was very interesting, like he runs the show, you know what I mean? He's the boss."

Nicole Kidman, who plays Kaitlyn in "Lioness," was also asked whether her character felt remorse over Oleksandra's death during an interview with Entertainment Weekly.

"She absolutely has a moral code and conscience, but she always weighs it up against cost. At the same time, she’s not mired down in regret. She’s a move-forward person, in the same way that when people play sports, you don’t get stuck on a previous point. Because otherwise she can’t do her job; she’s rendered inactive and vulnerable then," Kidman told the outlet.

Neretin also described Sheridan's writing and production process as an interesting experience.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"So we don't have all the episodes right away. So that was an interesting process. Because this is my first big role, I didn't know that that's how he worked. So that part was interesting because I didn't know. And it's like, you're waiting, and it feels like Christmas every time the episode drops. You're like, ‘Oh my God.’ And that's all we talk about on set the next day, everybody's like, 'Oh my gosh, did you see this?' Yeah, people have bets going what's gonna happen," she said.

A fourth season of "Lioness" has not been confirmed, but Kidman believes Kaitlyn's story could take many different paths if the series returns.

"There’s a lot. We’ll see where it goes, if we get to make a fourth season. It’s just so rich that there’s so many different paths that you can go down. The first season, you’re establishing everything, and the beauty of getting to do multiple seasons is that it becomes more deeper, richer, more complex. Taylor is such a strong writer that he can take things anywhere," she said.

item.title: New Jersey police pull out 3-foot python from woman's car grille, bodycam video shows
item.description: Body camera footage shows New Jersey police dismantling a car's front bumper to free a 3-foot ball python wedged inside the vehicle's grille.
item.content:encoded:
A New Jersey woman got a slithery surprise when she returned home from a wheel alignment and discovered a 3-foot python wedged inside the front grille of her car — prompting police to dismantle part of the vehicle to free the reptile.

Aiyana Hudson made the startling discovery on Sept. 14 in Franklin Township and called police for help, according to WABC-TV.

Body camera footage showed responding officers inspecting the car and working to determine how to safely remove the snake.

Officer Lisseth Villacis told the outlet that police initially contacted animal control but were told the agency only handled domesticated animals.

SURPRISE TRAVELER TRAPPED BENEATH CAR FOR HUNDREDS OF MILES GETS NEW CHANCE AT LIFE

"We tried getting animal control out there, and they're like, they only deal with domesticated animals," Villacis said. "And we're like, oh shoot. OK. So, we're kind of like the last resort."

Officers then took matters into their own hands, removing parts of the vehicle, including the front bumper, to reach the trapped reptile, as seen in the footage.

After about 20 minutes, police managed to untangle and safely free the snake, which animal control officials identified as a 3-foot ball python.

HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL PLAYER PRACTICES WITH VENOMOUS SNAKE HIDING INSIDE HELMET BEFORE COACH'S DISCOVERY

Hudson said she was relieved the unexpected passenger never found its way inside the vehicle while she was in it.

"I was just really happy that it didn't, like, pop its head through the AC vent when I was driving or come in through the steering wheel," Hudson told the outlet. "I want to let you know my car would have been lit on fire, and we'd be calling the fire department at that point."

How the python ended up in the grille remains unclear.

The snake was unharmed and taken to the Franklin Township Animal Shelter, according to MyCentralJersey.com.

Franklin Township Public Safety Director Lloyd Fredericks also reminded residents that releasing exotic pets into the wild is illegal and can pose a threat to native wildlife and household pets. Residents who have pet snakes and can no longer care for them should surrender it to the township animal shelter, he said.

item.title: Boston Globe op-ed says violence against transgender people is 'going down' despite activist claims
item.description: A Boston Globe opinion piece cited data from the Advocates for Trans Equality and the Human Rights Campaign showing a significant drop in violent transgender deaths.
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Globe published an opinion piece on Tuesday declaring that violence against transgender people was "going down" under President Donald Trump, contrary to warnings from transgender advocacy groups.

The article, written by former USA Today columnist David Mastio, cited statistics from Advocates for Trans Equality and the Human Rights Campaign (HRC) that Mastio said showed substantial declines in recorded violent deaths in recent years. Despite this, Mastio noted that the organizations have continued warning about violence against transgender people.

"Advocacy groups insist the data is incomplete and shouldn’t be used to draw any conclusions about the prevalence of anti-trans violence," Mastio wrote. "That’s due, they say, to the bigotry of families and authorities who misname and misgender the victims, making it hard to discern from public records how many transgender people are dying."

MOTHER JONES' WNBA 'TRANS PANIC' STORY SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN ACTIVISM MASQUERADES AS JOURNALISM

The article's headline read, "In Trump’s America, violence against transgender people isn’t going up — it’s going down." 

He continued, "Still it’s hard to imagine that as awareness about the transgender community has grown, misgendering and pronoun-swapping have become more common in police reports and news accounts than they were a decade ago, when another prominent LGBTQ organization, the Human Rights Campaign, began publishing its own numbers on violence against transgender people. The HRC tallies, too, find a declining number of violent transgender deaths to mourn. The group found a peak in 2021 of 47 deaths falling to 27 last year. HRC described that 40 percent drop as an 'ongoing onslaught of violence.'"

Mastio wrote, "But despite a hostile Trump administration and a barrage of anti-trans legislation across the country, the number of violent deaths the group documents has fallen nearly 50 percent from 53 in 2023 to 27 in 2025."

Mastio also cited a report from the Manhattan Institute, which asserted that the transgender population actually has a lower murder rate than the population as a whole. He added that the HRC did not respond to a request for comment when asked to rebut the report.

The report was written by Vincent Lundgren and Manhattan Institute fellow Colin Wright.

Fox News Digital reached out to the HRC for comment.

The Advocates for Trans Equality told Fox News Digital that a "dip in one datapoint" does not suggest that transgender people are any safer today.

DOUG SCHOEN: WHY DEMOCRATS CANNOT BREAK FREE FROM THE FAR LEFT’S TRANSGENDER DEMANDS

"Anyone claiming trans people are safer today under the Trump administration is ignoring what’s happening. Right now, everyone in this country, trans people included, is facing Medicaid cuts, soaring gas prices, ICE terrorizing our communities, and attacks on the right to vote. On top of that, attacks on trans people have been relentless," the organization said.

It continued, "This year alone, lawmakers across the country introduced over 700 anti-trans bills. Trans people are being cut off from gender-affirming care, denied IDs that match who they are, and housed in prisons that don’t match their gender. Any one of these makes trans people less safe. Together, they are a deliberate, hateful attack on the trans community under this administration, and people will die because of it."

Manhattan Institute fellow Colin Wright called the Globe column a "shockingly sober article" that cited his report and said he was not surprised the HRC did not respond to Mastio.

PRISHA MOSELY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME

"That's unsurprising because the HRC is engaging in fundraising propaganda. They don't care about the truth, only promoting the narrative. Our report presenting the actual data is irrefutable. That's why they have nothing to say in response," Wright wrote on X.

In comments to Fox News Digital, Wright said he was glad to see a mainstream outlet report on his data and hoped the article marked a turning point for the media.

"I do hope this is a sign that the media is no longer being held hostage by activists and is slowly being allowed to think again. At the Manhattan Institute, we believe that real justice requires an unwavering commitment to the truth. We have presented that truth in our report, and now the media must decide whether to acknowledge it or hide from it," Wright said.

The Boston Globe told Fox News Digital in a statement, "This is a guest op-ed. The views expressed in the piece are those of the author. Globe Opinion publishes a wide range of viewpoints and perspectives."

item.title: WWE legend Kurt Angle provides 'crazy' detail about iconic 'milk-o-mania' moment
item.description: Kurt Angle revealed the iconic Attitude Era milk truck segment on "Monday Night Raw" didn't actually use real milk, exposing a key WWE secret.
item.content:encoded:
The Attitude Era in WWE, then known as the World Wrestling Federation, provided some of the wildest moments in pro wrestling history. With those must-see segments, the company was able to win the "Monday Night Wars" and buy out its competition.

Kurt Angle was a main figure in some of those showcases and helped lead WWE into its Ruthless Aggression Era. One moment that sticks out more than most was the time Angle doused the "Stone Cold" Steve Austin-led alliance.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

After WWE brought in World Championship Wrestling (WCW) and Extreme Championship Wrestling (ECW) wrestlers, The Alliance was formed as part of an "invasion" angle. Angle was leading the charge for the WWE. The group showed appreciation for Austin on the Aug. 20, 2001, edition of "Monday Night Raw."

Angle interrupted the ceremony by driving a milk truck down to the ring. He connected a hose to the truck and doused everyone in the ring with what everyone thought was milk.

"Milk-o-Mania is running wild," then-WWE commentator Jim Ross said during the segment.

When OutKick Dropkick asked Angle what his favorite type of milk was, he revealed a key detail about the segment. It wasn’t actually milk that he sprayed during the moment.

"My milk of choice is 2%. But that wasn't really milk. That was food coloring," he said on behalf of Gambling.com, the guide to the best online sportsbooks. "What they did, it is pretty cool, the hose that we had hooked up it had food coloring in the right front where the spicket is or where the knob is. And when the water would go through, it would turn white.

"So, everybody thought it was milk and you know what's crazy is it wasn't. But it looked like milk. When I was drinking the milk and chugging it down, that was real milk. But it was crazy because a lot of people think that the hose that was spraying ‘Stone Cold’ Steve Austin and Stephanie McMahon down was real milk and it wasn't."

The spot is still one of the most-talked-about moments of Angle’s career and it definitely had this journalist fooled at the old age of nine.

Angle had a storied career in WWE.

He was a six-time world champion, won the Intercontinental Championship, European Championship, Hardcore Championship, United States Championship and Tag Team Championship one-time each and was the 2000 King of the Ring. He was the fifth person to be recognized as a Grand Slam champion.

Angle was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2017.

item.title: Pro-life leader sounds alarm after doctor gets 6 months for forcing abortion pills on girlfriend
item.description: Marjorie Dannenfelser slams the six-month sentence for Hassan-James Abbas, who forced crushed abortion pills into his pregnant girlfriend's mouth.
item.content:encoded:
Marjorie Dannenfelser, the president of SBA Pro-Life America, told Fox News Digital that U.S. law has not caught up with the growing availability of abortion medication, allowing predators who use the drugs to end pregnancies without women’s consent to face relatively light consequences.

She pointed to the case of Hassan-James Abbas, an Ohio man accused of forcing abortion pills into his pregnant girlfriend's mouth in December 2024. He was sentenced earlier this month to six months in prison.

The woman, Jona Affholder, went to the hospital and ultimately lost the baby.

"The fact that this guy got only six months in prison for his crime says a lot about the state of our culture right now," Dannenfelser said. "This was a very much wanted pregnancy. She could support the baby on her own and didn't need his help. But he had other ideas in mind."

PRO-LIFE CEO PREDICTS TRUMP FDA NOMINEE COULD BRING RENEWED SCRUTINY TO ABORTION DRUG RISKS

Abbas, then a surgical resident at the University of Toledo, began dating Affholder in early October 2024, according to a lawsuit she filed against him.

Sometime in December that year, Affholder got pregnant. Authorities said once he found out, he illegally obtained mifepristone and misoprostol using his estranged wife's identification information. It is unclear whether Abbas prescribed the drugs himself.

Taken together, the two medications terminate early pregnancies: mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain the pregnancy, while misoprostol causes contractions that expel the fetus.

TRUMP-BACKED VIVEK RAMASWAMY WINS OHIO GOP GUBERNATORIAL PRIMARY, WILL FACE DEMOCRAT AMY ACTON

Under current FDA rules, patients do not have to see a physician in person to receive a prescription, allowing mifepristone to be prescribed after a telehealth visit and mailed by a certified pharmacy.

After getting his hands on the pills, he began offering Affholder hot chocolate and tea, "which was out of character for their relationship," according to the Lucas County Prosecutor's Office.

On Dec. 18, 2024, Abbas invited her to his home in Holland, Ohio. Prosecutors said despite being aware of Affholder's intention to keep the baby, he climbed on top of her in bed, held her down and shoved crushed abortion pills into her mouth.

Court records show that when Affholder tried to call 911, he took the phone out of her hand and hung it up. Eventually, she was able to leave Abbas's residence and get to the hospital.

Affholder described this experience in a Daily Wire op-ed published in June 2026.

HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS

"I fought him off and ran to call 911. He took my cell and my keys, blocking me from leaving. I rushed to the kitchen, trying to rinse the powder from my mouth. But he continued to restrain me, buying each minute for the drugs to do their intended purpose of killing our kid," Affholder wrote.

"When he assumed the drugs had sufficiently aborted our baby, he returned my belongings, and I went straight to the hospital," she added. 

According to Affholder's account, she began hemorrhaging after arriving at the hospital and ultimately miscarried.

Abbas, who was arrested the next day, initially pleaded not guilty. In May 2026, he pleaded no contest to four felony charges: disrupting public services, unlawfully distributing abortion-inducing drugs, identity fraud and using deception to obtain a dangerous drug.

As part of the plea agreement, prosecutors dropped charges of abduction and tampering with evidence. The state had alleged that Abbas drove away from the home on the night of the assault and threw the remaining pills out his car window.

BLUE STATE SHIELD LAWS ALLOWED 330K ABORTION PILLS TO BE SENT TO ABORTION BAN STATES, PRO-LIFE GROUP FINDS

Dannenfelser contrasted Abbas' six-month sentence with Ohio's penalties for rape, which can carry years or even life in prison depending on the circumstances.

"But... this coercion and this attack that led to the death of her wanted child gets only six months," she said.

In February 2024, Mason Herring, of Texas, received the exact same sentence — six months — for slipping misoprostol into his then wife's drinks. The baby survived but initially faced severe developmental delays.

"If you are Amy Acton running for governor [of Ohio], if you are Sherrod Brown running for the Senate, you need to answer for this because their Republican opponents are very much for limiting these drugs or controlling them at least," Dannenfelser added.

Fox News Digital reached out to both campaigns for comment.

Dannenfelser also criticized Planned Parenthood and pro-choice advocates, accusing them of failing to speak out about Affholder’s case and others like it.

"Where are the advocates, the feminists, the people who are against the coercion of women, the people who are 'my body, my choice,' the people who say that medical care is all that they're really looking for," she said.

Planned Parenthood does not appear to have publicly commented on Affholder's case, but the organization has explicitly condemned the act of giving women abortion drugs without their knowledge or consent.

Fox News Digital reached out to Planned Parenthood for comment.

Dannenfelser said the Department of Justice should take a more active role in prosecuting cases involving forced abortions.

"We do have every hope that the attorney general will move on this, and he's referenced it at the Dallas convention that people who are pushing death in a pill will be disappointed," she said. "That is the surest way to justice."

On Tuesday, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, joined Dannenfelser in demanding Attorney General Todd Blanche take action, referencing Affholder's case.

"My constituent was held down and force-fed crushed-up mail-order abortion pills," Moreno wrote to Blanche. "Unsurprisingly, reckless Biden-era mail-in abortion policies are responsible for this hell-on-earth tragedy."

item.title: How the 'Squatter Hunter' is fighting home takeovers with tech
item.description: Flash Shelton reveals how home security cameras and alarm systems can stop squatters before they claim tenant rights in your vacant property.
item.content:encoded:
You leave a home empty while you travel, prepare it for sale or help an aging parent move. Then an unfamiliar car appears in the driveway. Someone gets inside. Before long, that person may even claim to have a lease. That kind of situation turned Flash Shelton into the man now known as the "Squatter Hunter." I recently sat down with Shelton on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast to talk about how his unusual line of work began and what homeowners can do before an unwanted occupant settles in.

He stars in A&E's "Squatters," which follows him and his team as they help property owners reclaim homes from unauthorized occupants. What stood out during our conversation was how often his advice came back to technology. A camera alert or alarm can give you something that becomes much harder to get later: evidence of when someone showed up and how they got inside.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

HOMEOWNERS TERRORIZED BY PRO SQUATTERS TURNING DREAMS INTO NIGHTMARES IN PALM-LINED PARADISE, EXPERTS SAY

Shelton says none of this started as a business idea. After his father died in 2019, he moved his mother in with him while preparing her vacant home for sale. Then seven people took over the property. Shelton told me he was "just being a good son" and felt he had to protect his mother after the squatters took advantage of the empty house. He called the sheriff and says he was told there was little law enforcement could do because the situation had become a civil issue. Shelton knew almost nothing about squatting at the time, but he did not accept that answer. "I was like, screw that. I'm going to do something about it," he recalled. He started researching how squatters operate and when occupancy claims can become harder to untangle.

His approach was unconventional. His mother, who owned the house, signed a legitimate lease giving Shelton the right to occupy the property. Shelton says he wanted documentation showing he had permission to be there in case the squatters produced a fake lease of their own. He then waited for the occupants to leave and entered the house using his key. Once inside, he started installing cameras and a security system. His thinking, he said, was that "if they can take a house, I can take a house." When some of the occupants returned, Shelton told them he had possession of the property and gave them until the end of the day to remove their furniture. He says cars and trucks soon arrived, and the house was cleared. Years later, that experience has turned into a full-time mission and an A&E series.

Squatting can create a serious and expensive problem for homeowners, even though there is no reliable nationwide count showing exactly how often it happens. Part of the challenge is how these cases are tracked. Squatting does not appear as its own category in national crime databases, and cases can be handled differently depending on whether authorities view them as trespassing, fraud or a landlord-tenant dispute. That makes it difficult to put one national number on the problem.

What we do know is that lawmakers across the country have been responding. As of July 2026, the National Apartment Association reported that 28 states had enacted laws addressing squatting. Another 25 states have introduced or considered legislation during 2026. Those measures include faster removal procedures and new penalties for some forms of unauthorized occupancy. There are also documented cases showing how disruptive squatting can become. A New York City Department of Investigation review found unauthorized occupants in 548 vacant NYCHA apartments. Joint DOI and NYPD operations reclaimed 60 of those apartments and resulted in 81 arrests involving unauthorized occupants accused of criminal activity connected with the properties.

So while there is no single number showing how many homes are affected nationwide, the growing legislative response and documented cases make one thing clear: unauthorized home takeovers are a real problem, and homeowners have good reason to think about prevention before a property sits empty.

LAKE TAHOE SQUATTER SUSPECT CAUGHT ON SURVEILLANCE IN RICH-AND-FAMOUS MOUNTAIN RETREAT

For all the unusual tactics Shelton has used since becoming the "Squatter Hunter," his biggest piece of advice is surprisingly simple. Put cameras on a vacant property before there is a problem. Looking back at his mother's home, Shelton told me, "If I had cameras on my mom's house back then, I wouldn't be the squatter hunter today." The back door had been broken. What Shelton lacked was proof showing exactly when the entry happened and who did it.

He believes footage could have changed the situation from the beginning. With cameras, Shelton said, he could have shown authorities, "on this date, at this time, and this is the person." That is where today's home technology can make a real difference. A connected camera can alert you when somebody approaches a house. It can record an entry. It can also give law enforcement a timeline before competing stories about who belongs there begin.

One of the biggest challenges can appear after someone gets inside. Shelton says experienced squatters may produce a lease and claim they were given permission to live there. "They know that if they get into a property and show a lease and create reasonable doubt," Shelton told me, law enforcement may refer the property owner to the courts instead of immediately removing the occupant.

That is another reason camera footage can become so useful. A document may say one thing. Video showing someone forcing a door or entering a clearly vacant home can provide additional evidence about what actually happened. Shelton says many of the people he encounters understand how housing rules work and try to use tenant protections to delay removal.

You hear the phrase "squatters' rights" constantly, but it can blur together very different legal concepts. Adverse possession generally requires someone to occupy property openly for a period set by state law while meeting other specific requirements. That can take years. Shelton says the disputes he deals with tend to revolve around something much more immediate: whether an unauthorized occupant can create enough uncertainty to be treated as a tenant.

"Squatters are doing everything they can to gain tenant rights," Shelton told me. "They're not interested in squatter laws or rights. They want tenant rights." That helps explain why the legal response varies so much by state. Some states have created faster procedures for owners who say an unauthorized person took over a property. Others have increased penalties for fake leases or fraudulent documents.

ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS

Shelton has dealt with situations that sound much more disturbing than somebody slipping into an abandoned property. During our interview, he described a case involving an 88-year-old woman in Culver City, California, who had hired a caregiver. According to Shelton, the caregiver lost the job but refused to leave the home. He said the situation eventually required intervention through social services and described it as a case involving elder abuse.

That experience sticks with him because the homeowner was especially vulnerable. Shelton has also worked on expensive properties. He recalled one Malibu home worth roughly $8 million and another case involving a Hollywood Hills mansion. His point was that there is no single profile of a property that can attract an unauthorized occupant. The same goes for the people involved. "They don't have a look," Shelton told me. "Squatters are your neighbors."

Watching Shelton confront people makes compelling television. Copying what you see on A&E could put you in a dangerous situation. The laws governing trespassing, tenancy and removal vary by state. If you discover somebody inside your property, call law enforcement and document what you can safely. Save camera footage. Preserve records showing when the property became vacant. Keep documentation identifying anyone who had permission to be there. If someone claims to be a tenant, an attorney familiar with local property law can help determine the appropriate next move.

Shelton brings years of experience into these encounters. He also has experience with de-escalation, which is another reminder that the confrontations you see on television come with risks. That is very different from a homeowner walking into a house alone and confronting a stranger.

The growing attention around squatting has turned Shelton into a television personality and given him more cases than he can handle. But he says his long-term goal goes in the opposite direction. "There are no shortage of cases" where people need help, he told me. Still, Shelton said, "I ultimately want to change these laws and put myself out of business."

In the meantime, his biggest message for homeowners has less to do with dramatic confrontations. Pay attention early. A camera can tell you someone arrived. An alarm can tell you a door opened. A neighbor can tell you a moving truck has suddenly pulled into the driveway. Once somebody has spent time inside and starts claiming the right to be there, the situation can become much more complicated.

NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE'

During our conversation, I kept asking Shelton the question most homeowners probably have: What can I actually do before this happens? His advice focuses on making a vacant property easier to monitor while reducing the signs that nobody is around.

Start with cameras covering the most likely entry points. Shelton likes the fact that systems today allow homeowners to check their property remotely. As he told me, "you can be anywhere in the world" and monitor what is happening at home from your phone. Look for motion alerts and person detection. Night vision can help when someone arrives after dark. Also check how your recordings are stored. If an incident occurs, save important clips so they do not disappear when a cloud-storage retention period expires. You can see my picks for the 12 best outdoor security cameras at CyberGuy.com.

A camera becomes a lot less useful if the electricity goes down. Shelton says he often works with battery-powered cameras because properties do not always have active power or internet access. Some batteries can keep a camera running for weeks or months, depending on the model and how frequently it records. He also recommends checking the backup capabilities of an alarm system. Before leaving a property vacant, Shelton told me to "make sure you've got cameras, your alarm system, everything's up-to-date." That means testing the system before you leave instead of assuming last year's setup still works. For a more complete setup, see my Best Home Security Systems 2026 guide at CyberGuy.com.

Shelton recommends timers for indoor lights and solar-powered security lighting when permanent power presents a problem. He also likes rechargeable lights with battery backup. That way, the house does not suddenly go completely dark during an outage. A smart plug or connected bulb can also let you adjust lighting remotely. The goal is to avoid broadcasting that a property has been sitting untouched.

One of Shelton's most practical tips costs nothing. Tell trusted neighbors when a house will be vacant and make it clear whether anybody has permission to enter. As Shelton put it, "Your neighbors, they don't want you to have a squatter either." Ask them to contact you if an unfamiliar vehicle repeatedly appears in the driveway or someone begins carrying furniture inside. Shelton relied on a neighbor himself at his mother's house. The property had no Wi-Fi, so a neighbor allowed him to use a nearby connection for his camera. That option will depend on range and the equipment involved, but the larger lesson still works. A neighbor can notice activity before you ever receive a call from anyone else.

Shelton says people scouting vacant properties can pay attention to mailboxes. An overflowing box may signal that nobody has been around. He also worries about an unauthorized occupant receiving mail at an address and later presenting it as evidence that they live there. "Make sure you have a mailbox that is lockable," Shelton advised. If you are traveling, arrange to have your mail held or picked up. Also, pay attention if correspondence begins arriving for unfamiliar people at a property that should be empty. Our CyberGuy vacation guide has more on mail holds and home security before a trip: 6 things to do before you leave on vacation.

Putting up a no-trespassing sign sounds obvious. Shelton says homeowners should find out whether their local law enforcement agency offers an additional step. He told me that some sheriff's departments allow owners to file a form documenting that a property has been posted against trespassing. Why bother? A person can pull a sign down. Shelton described the thinking pretty simply: someone sees the notice, removes it and later says, "What sign?" Having something on file with local authorities may help document the owner's wishes even if the physical notice disappears. Procedures vary, so check directly with your local sheriff or police department before relying on this strategy.

SAN FRANCISCO HOME WITH HISTORY OF SQUATTERS UNDER CONTRACT FOR $1.3 MILLION

Shelton also recommends thinking about the clues people can see from the street. Put lights on timers. Keep the yard maintained. Avoid leaving packages outside. If practical, Shelton suggests leaving a vehicle in the driveway. He even recommends asking a trusted friend whether they can park there while you are away. None of that guarantees somebody will stay away. It can make a vacant property less obvious to a person scouting for an easy target.

If you plan to be gone for a week or longer, Shelton recommends doing one final security check before you leave. "Make sure you've got cameras, your alarm system, everything's up-to-date," he told me. Check camera batteries. Make sure motion alerts reach your phone. Confirm that your alarm is communicating properly. Also think about what happens if someone cuts the power or the neighborhood has an outage. Shelton recommends equipment with battery backup whenever possible. A few minutes spent testing everything before you leave could prevent you from discovering later that the camera you were counting on stopped recording days earlier.

A squatter moving into a property does not automatically gain legal ownership of it. However, homeowners should also be aware of a separate threat called home title fraud. Criminals can use fraudulent documents or stolen personal information to try to change property records or obtain financing tied to a home.

That makes property-record monitoring another layer of protection. A home title monitoring service can alert you to certain changes involving your property records, including a new owner, new lender or changes in financing. Home title monitoring cannot stop someone from entering your property or prevent a fraudulent filing. However, an alert can help you spot an unexpected change and investigate it sooner. See my tips and best picks on home title monitoring services at CyberGuy.com.

What happened at Flash Shelton's mother's house shows how quickly a vacant property can become somebody else's opportunity. For me, the most useful part of his story comes before any confrontation. Shelton wishes he had cameras running when people first entered his mother's home. That says a lot. The sooner you know somebody has entered your property, the sooner you can call for help and preserve evidence showing what happened. I also would not overlook the low-tech advice. Tell a trusted neighbor when a property should be empty. Pay attention to the mailbox. Find out what your local police or sheriff recommends before you need them. And remember that the law is changing quickly. With 28 states now having enacted measures addressing squatting, you should check the rules where your property is located rather than assuming something you saw online applies everywhere. You can hear my full conversation with Flash Shelton on The CyberGuy Report podcast.

Should states make it easier for homeowners to remove squatters quickly, or could tougher laws go too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: FCC chair blasts House Democrats 'extreme position' on gender ideology in kids' programming in fiery letter
item.description: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr fired back at House Democrats who opposed the agency's push to reform children's TV ratings over content pushing gender ideology.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX — The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr on Tuesday issued a fiery response to the opposition from House Democrats over the agency's effort to reform television ratings for children's programming, some of which promotes gender ideology.

In April, the FCC issued a public notice seeking feedback about parents' concern about the content of shows their children watch, suggesting the current ratings system is outdated and deems "shows with transgender and gender non-binary programming as appropriate for children and young children" and that new ratings may be necessary.

That prompted a response in June from Democrats on the Congressional Equality Caucus, who accused the FCC of wanting to "censor the inclusion of transgender characters or topics" from children's programming and said that the current ratings system is "satisfactory and overwhelmingly popular among parents."

WASHINGTON FATHER SUES SCHOOL DISTRICT FOR DENYING RELIGIOUS OPT-OUT FOR 5TH GRADER FROM LGBTQ INSTRUCTION

"We strongly believe that parents should decide what their children watch on television," the lawmakers wrote. "Programs should not have higher ratings or content warning simply because of the identity of the programs’ characters. Applying higher ratings or content warnings because of a character’s gender identity would be harmful to transgender people and transgender acceptance and would harken back to a time when politicians sought to censor television programming because they included minorities."

The House Democrats continued, "Any attempt by FCC to censor content because it includes transgender characters or topics would raise both legal and constitutional concerns... Any attempt to issue rating warnings for depictions and themes related to transgender people would also raise concerns of content-based and viewpoint discrimination in violation of the First Amendment."

BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

In a letter sent Tuesday to Congressional Equality Caucus Chair Rep. Mark Takano, D-Calif., Carr expressed regret for the stance the Democratic lawmakers had taken.

"I am deeply concerned by the position that you and over 60 of your Democrat colleagues in the House of Representatives are taking regarding the right of parents to know whether their sons or daughters are being exposed to controversial gender identity ideologies—including the promotion of transgender and gender non-binary programming—in television shows that are rated as appropriate for young children," Carr began the letter obtained by Fox News Digital. 

"In your letter, you come out swinging against both transparency and common sense," Carr added. "You stake out the radical position that parents have no right to know whether controversial gender identity ideologies are being promoted in children’s television programming. In your view, parents should not be empowered to make informed choices about the programs their children watch."

Carr called the Democrats' defense of transgender people an "extreme position" which he said comes as children's programming is "secretly promoting gender ideology to young kids without the knowledge or consent of their parents."

He went on to list several examples of gender ideology appearing in children's programming, citing an episode of Disney Jr.'s "Muppet Babies" reboot (TV-Y) where Gonzo wants to dress as a princess instead of a knight, calls himself "Gonzo-rella" and is referred to in the episode with the "they" pronoun, as well as a trans character in Netflix's "Strawberry Shortcake: Berry in the Big City" (TV-Y) and pansexual and non-binary characters in the Disney Channel's animated series "Primos" (TV-Y7).

"Keeping parents in the dark about the nature of these programs is a feature not a bug of the effort. Indeed, you write in your letter that 'many recognize their gender identity at a young age.' And you appear to suggest that informing parents would prevent 'self-acceptance,'" Carr wrote. "Recent studies show a massive spike in younger people identifying as transgender with some attributing this to media exposure. But your position that New York and Hollywood programmers should have a direct line to children without parental knowledge is at total odds with the law Congress passed."

"Opposing transparency puts you on the wrong side of the issue. Parents are nearly unanimous in wanting to know what their children are watching and to determine for their own families what shows are appropriate. Despite your opposition, the FCC will continue its work to empower parents and continue to engage with stakeholders as part of the agency’s open and ongoing proceeding," Carr added.

Rep. Takano's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Fox News' Brian Flood contributed to this report.

item.title: Lost in translation: Israel, Huckabee blast Macron over Hamas comments as France clarifies wording
item.description: President Donald Trump vowed Iran will never have a nuclear weapon as United Nations leaders accused Israel of war crimes and forced displacement.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump offered a roaring counterbalance to a spate of world leaders bashing Israel or appearing to equivocate between the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attacks and Jerusalem’s response — as one world leader was assailed for his comments on Hamas.

Gaza dominated the opening day of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, despite a ceasefire, as world leaders accused Israel of continuing to displace Palestinians and undermine prospects for peace. 

French President Emmanuel Macron accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank, questioning the justification for its actions and making a remark that was translated as "Hamas was never active in the West Bank."

MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT

Israeli U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon challenged his claim about Hamas’ presence in the West Bank. "French President Emmanuel Macron claimed from the UN podium that Hamas has ‘never been active’ in Judea and Samaria. Just two days ago, a French citizen was murdered there," Danon wrote on X. "Mr. President, Emmanuel Macron, do your homework before lecturing Israel. Check the facts."

Asked by Fox News Digital to clarify Macron’s remarks, a French Foreign Ministry spokesperson said: "The president meant to say that Hamas does not govern the West Bank. His remarks should therefore not be misinterpreted."

In response to the comments, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee reposted Israel's Minister of Diaspora and Combating Antisemitism. Huckabee stated, "Hard to imagine a more out of touch with reality speech than Macron at UN. @AmichaiChikli corrects the record. Hamas is an evil scourge, and they have killed innocent American citizens.

Chickli's post noted in part that, "Since 1990, Hamas has carried out more than 80 lethal terrorist attacks originating in or directed from Judea and Samaria, murdering more than 350 Israeli civilians." Judea and Samaria is another term used for the West Bank.

Macron also accused Israel of violating Palestinian rights in the West Bank and undermining the sovereignty of neighboring Lebanon, where he said villages in the south were being "razed." Macron questioned the credibility of the international community’s recognition of Palestinian statehood if it failed to act on the situation in Gaza. "Some claim that peace has been achieved," he said, calling the situation "shameful."

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, in his final address to the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) as secretary-general, opened fire on Israel’s response in Gaza, describing it as "a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as Secretary-General."

"Amid the turmoil engulfing the region, we must not lose sight of the devastating situation in the Occupied Palestinian Territory," he said, as the world approaches three years since the Hamas terror attacks that sparked the Israeli military response he spent much of his speech criticizing.

At the same time, Guterres lamented the ongoing conflict in Sudan, saying the war-torn East African nation is a place the "world looks away" from wrongly.

Yet his decision to single out Gaza as "the worst" devastation he had witnessed during his tenure raised questions about the international community's uneven attention to two of the world's deadliest conflicts. Approximately 72,000 Palestinians have been reported killed in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run Health Ministry, compared with an estimated 150,000 people killed in Sudan's civil war. Many of those killed in Gaza include terrorists.

King Abdullah II of Jordan, a regional U.S. ally whose country signed a peace agreement with Israel in 1994, doubled down on the anti-Israel tenor, accusing Jerusalem of "war crimes."

"In my region, from Lebanon to Yemen, to Sudan, protracted conflict is deepening humanitarian suffering," Abdullah said. "And if anyone had any doubt that a crisis in our part of the world stays there, just look at the energy and grocery bills of ordinary families, from Mumbai to Madrid to Minnesota."

WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR?

Abdullah said Jordanian field hospitals had been targeted during the first 300 days of the "so-called ceasefire" and lamented the deaths of Palestinian children.

He also praised Trump for "pushing hard for peace" while pivoting to fault Israel for "moving the goalposts" and allegedly destroying civilian infrastructure in Gaza.

"The question is, is this the behavior of a democratic state governed by law? What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts. It is elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land," Abdullah said.

"And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime."

Abdullah also accused Israel of harboring territorial ambitions in Syria, calling on the international community to act.

Just before Abdullah, President Donald Trump offered a scathing counterweight to the invective directed at the Netanyahu administration and Israel’s response to Palestinian terrorism.

BRITAIN’S DRAMATIC CRACKDOWN ON ISRAELI SETTLEMENTS SPARKS FIERCE RESPONSE AS US BLOWBACK LOOMS

"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon" was a mantra repeated by Trump from the dais, as he noted that the Khamenei regime had also celebrated Oct. 7 as a "service to humanity" while murdering thousands of Iranian citizens in recent months, according to the president.

"Just imagine such a vile regime, wherever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront, the reality that far too many preferred to ignore," he said, taking occasional swipes at nations — and previous U.S. leaders — who refused to help neutralize the Iranian threat.

"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" he asked. "But I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election," he added, suggesting Iran is waiting to see whether Republicans retain control of Congress while noting that he himself is not on the ballot.

Meanwhile, criticism of Israel continued from the dais throughout the day.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said that former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and former Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat were "statesmen" who sought solutions with courage and clarity.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"They were defeated by hatred," Lula da Silva claimed, according to the U.N.’s transcript of his remarks.

"Generations of Palestinians will carry the pain and trauma left by the genocide of women and children perpetrated by Netanyahu[‘s] government in Gaza," he said.

Danon told Fox News Digital that, "Unfortunately, it’s not new, but the U.N. is obsessed with Israel."

"Instead of focusing and dealing with the real issues, they all gather and gang against Israel," he said. "[It is] the weakness of the secretary general. That is why we are grateful for President Trump, who came to the U.N., delivered a very powerful speech with moral clarity, but we are used to it… Unfortunately, instead of taking practical actions to improve the world, it's much easier to blame Israel about everything," he said.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, called Gaza "the world's biggest graveyard for children" and compared the situation there to Holocaust-era concentration camps, continuing his history of comparing Israel to Nazi Germany.

Danon said it is legitimate to criticize Israel and that its leaders welcome debate — but that the U.N. instead delved into "pure hate [and] incitement," singling out Erdoğan, who is supposed to be a Western ally.

"[He] comes here every year, compares the Israelis to the Nazis. That's shameful. That's shameful. And he shows that he's an antisemite. He doesn't really care about the Palestinians. He just wants to sow chaos and instigate against the Jewish people."

As for King Abdullah's remarks, Danon said, "He should know better. We work with Jordan, we support Jordan, we defended Jordan in the past. But unfortunately, many leaders, when they come here, they don't speak about the cooperation with Israel, the economical or security cooperation. They join the group and they always criticize us."

Fox News Digital's Hannah Brennan contributed to this report.

item.title: Mystery surrounds German soldiers found near mud-covered WWII motorcycle in Danube
item.description: A Wehrmacht motorcycle and the remains of two German soldiers have emerged from the Danube River in Budapest more than 80 years after World War II ended.
item.content:encoded:
A relic of World War II has emerged from the Danube more than 80 years after the war ended — along with the remains of two German soldiers whose identities still remain a mystery.

The Wehrmacht motorcycle — which officials identified as a DKW NZ 350-1 — was found in the Danube River in central Budapest this summer.

The discovery was announced by the German War Graves Commission, an organization that works to locate, recover and identify German war dead, in August.

WRECK OF DEADLIEST US NAVAL LOSS OF WORLD WAR I FOUND AFTER MORE THAN A CENTURY: 'LOST WITH ALL HANDS'

Pictures show the heavily corroded motorcycle caked in mud and rust — with its frame, wheels, fuel tank and storage boxes still largely intact.

"Because the harbor mud is mixed with gas oil, the motorcycle and identification tags are well preserved," the German War Graves Commission said in a statement, adding that the motorcycle model "was considered particularly robust and reliable at the time."

Officials also found the remains of two German soldiers while recovering the motorcycle, along with two well-preserved identification tags.

Both tags were still intact. 

Typically, one half of a fallen soldier's tag was left with the body, while the other was sent to the Wehrmacht Information Office so that the soldier's family could be notified, according to the commission.

EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

The identification tags found with the remains are still being deciphered, Diane Tempel-Bornett, a spokesperson for the German War Graves Commission, told Fox News Digital in a translated email.

Tempel-Bornett said that despite the discovery of the tags, the identities of the two soldiers remain unknown.

"The fact that the identification tags were found with the dead does not necessarily mean that they belonged to them — although that is quite possible," she said.

REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY

The fact that the tags were still intact could indicate the soldiers were never recovered or officially accounted for after their deaths, Tempel-Bornett said.

Tempel-Bornett said identifying the soldiers can be a "long, painstaking process," with even small details offering potential clues.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Investigators can glean clues from the remains, including height, age and possible origin, while personal belongings such as wedding rings, glasses, jewelry and papers can also help establish an identity. 

Researchers then compare those findings with military records and other historical evidence.

"Here, we work closely with the German Federal Archives in Berlin," she added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Only when everything fits together is the person's fate considered to have been clarified."

The final stage, Tempel-Bornett said, is to reach out to any relatives of the deceased.

"If we have inquiries from relatives searching for them, that makes it easier," she said. "Otherwise, our colleagues try to do so through an inquiry with the residents' registration authorities."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For now, the identities of the two soldiers — and how they and the motorcycle came to rest in the Danube — are an ongoing mystery.

"We can only speculate [on the cause of death]," added Tempel-Bornett.

"Whether the dead tried to cross the frozen Danube, whether one fell, whether the dead were shot or drowned … we will only know after their fate has been clarified."

item.title: Socialist mayor’s new answer to rampant retail crime ignites fury: ‘Bandage on a bullet wound’
item.description: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson's $1.7 million grocery store security plan draws fierce criticism from those demanding the city arrest and prosecute criminals.
item.content:encoded:
Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson is rolling out city-funded security for grocery stores facing theft, break-ins and vandalism, fueling criticism that Seattle is spending taxpayer money to protect businesses from crime instead of doing enough to stop it in the first place.

The socialist mayor announced the rollout of the security funding as part of a $1.7 million grocery-support initiative included in the city's 2026 budget earlier this week. 

"Keeping our neighborhood grocery stores safe and supported is essential to making sure every Seattleite has a reliable, affordable grocery store near them," Wilson said on social media Monday.

The plan will help 10 independent grocery stores pay for improvements and get a year of business support, while stores hit hard by retail theft can get one-time funding for security upgrades and repairs.

'WASTEFUL DISTRACTION': EXPERTS SLAM MAMDANI'S TAXPAYER-FUNDED GROCERY STORES

The security funding is already drawing criticism from conservatives who argue the city is spending public money to help businesses absorb the consequences of crime rather than focusing enough resources on preventing it.

"The best way to support grocery store — and all businesses — is to actually enforce the law with a fully staffed and funded police department. Giving money or resources to fix businesses that are broken by crime is a bandage on a bullet wound," Seattle-based KTTH host and conservative commentator Jason Rantz told Fox News Digital.

SMALL-BUSINESS OWNER URGES SEATTLE LEADERS TO ACT NOW ON PUBLIC DRUG USE AND SLOW EMERGENCY RESPONSE

"We don’t need to think outside the box here. Just enforce the law and put criminals in jail. That works like a charm and will save everyone money and headaches," Rantz added.

"Is there no single human in Seattle willing to identify the criminals and end the crime instead," asked an X user.

"Seattle is arguably the worst city in the entire country right now, in terms of the rampant crime, widespread degradation and lawlessness that’s apparently gotten exponentially worse across the board over the last 2-3 yrs," another user chimed in.

NEW YORK SOCIALIST LAWMAKER TAKES HEAT AFTER SAYING SHOPLIFTING RESULTS FROM 'BIOLOGICAL NEED'

"That used to be called the police department. What are these security guards going to do? Make arrests? Observe & report? The criminals will walk right past the security with their stolen goods. If they detain they will be sued. Cops will not arrest the shoplifters or prosecute," said one person.

"Goodness! imagine how much nicer the city would be if they simply arrested and charged criminals and put them in jail? Normal people shouldn't have to shop at stores with security guards. NONE of this was necessary in most parts of Seattle 15 years ago," wrote an X user.

"So we are working around the problem by increasing security instead of arresting the problem," said another person.

The city will also work with the Independent Grocers Alliance to study eight neighborhoods for potential new grocery stores, according to the plan.

Wilson floated the idea of exploring a "public option" for grocery stores during her 2025 mayoral campaign, including models that could involve publicly supported or city-run grocery stores. While the new initiative is separate from those proposals, critics argued the city should focus more heavily on arresting and prosecuting retail thieves rather than spending additional money helping stores deal with the damage caused by crime.

The grocery security funding was first proposed by former Mayor Bruce Harrell as $1 million for grocery-store security in his 2026 budget, specifically targeting retail theft, property damage and other crimes.

City leaders pushed to cut police spending amid the 2020 "Black Lives Matter" movement and the city subsequently experienced a steep decline in police staffing, with the department falling from 1,424 officers in 2019 to 1,054 in 2024 before hiring began to rebound, the Seattle Mayor's Office previously reported. 

The broader theft problem remains significant in Seattle, where police recorded nearly 7,500 larceny-theft offenses across the city's five precincts through May, making it the most commonly reported crime category in every precinct.

Fox News Digital reached out to the mayor's office on Tuesday.

item.title: Supreme Court declines to intervene in case of surrogate mother who refused abortion
item.description: McKenna West's surrogacy custody fight over a baby with hypoplastic left heart syndrome hit the Supreme Court after she fled to Texas to avoid an abortion.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined Tuesday to intervene in the case of a surrogate mother who refused to have an abortion and is now seeking custody of the child.

McKenna West gave birth to the boy, whom she named Gabriel, in Texas in August after she fled from California when the parents asked her to abort the child over a heart defect. She argued in Texas court that she should maintain custody over the child despite the surrogacy agreement, but a judge in Texas ruled against her.

West then appealed to the Supreme Court, but Justice Elena Kagan, who handles cases arising from California, declined to hear the case on Tuesday without issuing a written decision.

SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION

The intended parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, signed a surrogacy agreement with West in August 2025. They point to a clause in the agreement that allowed for a termination of pregnancy in the case of a "fetal abnormality."

The child, whom they had named Rumi, was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, which causes part of the heart to be underdeveloped and prevents normal blood flow. The child underwent surgery in Texas and is now "suffering from potential complications" related to the operation.

HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY

Ahmed and Gilkar attempted to force West to have an abortion when the defect was initially detected, but West refused and fled to Texas, where she received support from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Paxton signed an order stating that the child must receive lifesaving care in Texas. The case went up to the Texas Supreme Court, which ruled last week that the child could be moved to California, where the intended parents have lined up plans for medical care.

Ahmed and Gilkar first sought out a surrogacy agreement after attempts at in vitro fertilization failed.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump anti-fraud division's future rests with Senate Dems after bipartisan House win
item.description: Senate Democrats aren't keen on giving President Donald Trump a win with elections nearing, and Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., fears that political calculus may stifle his anti-fraud push.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: House Democrats paved the way for President Donald Trump's anti-fraud division to survive beyond his presidency, but one Republican fears it'll be a different outcome in the Senate. 

Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., shared with Fox News Digital that he was introducing legislation that would make the National Fraud Enforcement Division permanent. It comes after a bill to do the same thing cruised through the House. The lawmaker made it official Tuesday night when the Senate reopened for business.

But the Senate is a different political animal, and Democrats’ possible reticence to give Trump a win before the midterm elections may thwart his plan. Schmitt, during an interview with Fox News Digital, contended that since the sprawling Minnesota fraud scandal was unveiled earlier this year, Democrats have been on the back foot.

DEMOCRATS RELUCTANTLY HAND TRUMP MAJOR VICTORY ON FRAUD PROGRAM TARGETING TIM WALZ

"They're very defensive about it, and you know the fact is that you had — maybe it had something to do with this sort of toxic empathy or suicidal empathy [they] have done on immigration where you had these Somali fraudsters and maybe, maybe their instinct to defend every group of people that came here from somewhere else, even if they're defrauding the American people, overrode their logic."

Still, House Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., begrudgingly gave Trump a win last week and voted to make his anti-fraud task force permanent. That bipartisan vote comes as Democrats are reconciling with their messaging on rooting out waste, fraud and abuse.

And New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has increasingly been one of the progressive leaders of the party, warned Democrats had ceded ground on issues like quality of life and rooting out waste and fraud, and that finding waste had taken hold as a "right-wing concern" rather than an issue Democrats could champion.

DEMOCRATS BEGRUDGINGLY HAND TRUMP VICTORY ON TARIFFS IN SPRAWLING SANCTIONS BILL

"I know that we live in a hyper-partisan age, I get that," Schmitt said. "But there are some things I don't think should be partisan. Saving taxpayer money should be something we're all focused on."

"I mean these are criminals who, you know, are stealing from American taxpayers and the potential beneficiaries of important programs," he continued.

Trump first announced the creation of a new division within the Department of Justice (DOJ) to combat fraud in January 2026 following reports of staggering fraud taking place in the backyard of one of his political enemies: Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz.

TRUMP SAYS ANTI-FRAUD EFFORTS ARE UNCOVERING BILLIONS IN WASTE, CLAIMS SAVINGS COULD BALANCE BUDGET

The unit embedded in the DOJ was officially launched under then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, with the goal of targeting "fraud affecting the federal government, federally funded programs, and private citizens," according to a release by the administration.

It’s chaired by Vice President JD Vance, who Trump tapped to be his de facto fraud czar, and run by Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald.

Schmitt argued that "having permanence in the Department of Justice will be important so that, no matter who is president, that this remains a focus."

"To me, this shouldn't be a partisan issue at all," Schmitt said. "But sadly, we live in a world where Democrats aren't as focused on this, but I think we've got an administration that is."

And Schmitt leads the Senate’s Anti-Fraud Taskforce, launched in June, that includes only Republican members. That wasn’t by design.

He said that they had extended an invitation to "Republicans and Democrats alike," but only one side of the aisle accepted the call.

"I was a little surprised. I think some offices took a look at it and, for whatever reason, didn't want to be part of the effort," Schmitt said. "I don't understand that."

"But, you know, of course, the offer remains open if anybody wants to," he continued. "I just think that this is something that our people back home expect us to work together on. And I don't understand why you wouldn't want to be a part of an anti-fraud task force."

item.title: Man goes to doctor to prove he’s 'in perfect shape,' test reveals shocking diagnosis
item.description: A Louisiana musician's early prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 is now fueling his advocacy for earlier PSA screening despite current guideline debates.
item.content:encoded:
Joseph Wayne Singleton, a 45-year-old musician from Opelousas, Louisiana, shared how a routine physical led to an early diagnosis that saved his life.

When Singleton was 33, his wife urged him to schedule a more thorough physical. Although he underwent annual exams to maintain his commercial driver's license, she felt those checkups weren't comprehensive enough.

"My mentality was, ‘OK, to make my wife happy, I'm going to do this and prove to her that I'm in perfect shape,'" he told Fox News Digital.

JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS

Although Singleton was too young for prostate cancer screening, his doctor decided to run a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test.

"He couldn’t explain what made him do that, but he did," he said.

Singleton’s results came back revealing PSA levels that were "through the roof." After a biopsy, he was later diagnosed with prostate cancer.

"It was totally unexpected," he said. "No symptoms."

CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE

Singleton, who was treated at UT MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, Texas, said the doctors had never seen prostate cancer in someone so young.

After undergoing a prostatectomy to remove the prostate, Singleton said his relatively young age contributed to what he described as a "miraculous" recovery.

"A couple of weeks after having the prostatectomy, I was back on airplanes flying across the country doing shows with my band," he said. "It wasn't as bad as it possibly could have been."

"By the grace of God, I'm here now," Singleton reflected. "It was quite an eye-opener. It made me question myself ... a lot of ‘why me?'"

CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

Singleton added, "I’m still here after all those years, and there was definitely a purpose behind everything that happened."

Part of that purpose, Singleton said, is to advocate for earlier prostate cancer screening when appropriate.

"I came to the conclusion that because of the platform that I have, being a musician, that maybe it was meant for me to be an advocate," he said. "I'm having people reach out to me from all across the country [who are] finding out about my story ... and I think it's very important."

"This could have turned out so much worse had I not gotten tested early," he went on. "I hate to think what could have happened."

"If I could help prevent somebody else from going through what I might have gone through, worse than what I went through, that's the main goal."

While Singleton advocates for earlier prostate cancer screening in younger men, even without symptoms, current screening guidelines do not recommend it.

Robert Smith, Ph.D., senior vice president of cancer screening at the American Cancer Society in Atlanta, Georgia, confirmed that current prostate cancer screening procedures differ depending on the patient.

"The one thing most organizations agree on is that clinicians should discuss prostate cancer screening with men, emphasizing benefits, limitations and harms associated with screening, diagnosis and treatment, rather than issue a direct recommendation to undergo screening," he told Fox News Digital.

The recommended age to begin prostate cancer screening remains a topic of debate, with some guidelines suggesting as early as 45 and others recommending age 50 or 55 for average-risk men.

Recommendations for when to stop screening also vary, generally ranging from ages 69 to 75 or when life expectancy is less than 10 years. Guidelines also differ on screening frequency, ranging from annual testing to every two to four years.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

For men at higher risk, including Black men and those with a family cancer history, Smith noted that guidelines recommend more frequent screening, starting at 40 to 45 years old.

Prostate cancer screening guidelines have long emphasized weighing the benefits against the risks, including overdiagnosis, overtreatment and potential side effects such as urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction, Smith said.

"However, over this period, it has become clear that prostate cancer screening is more effective at reducing prostate cancer deaths than was previously believed, and there are new strategies ... to mitigate the harms associated with diagnosing and treating prostate cancer."

Guidelines on screening and treatment have evolved based on this new evidence and will likely continue to change, Smith noted.

The doctor said Singleton's diagnosis was concerning because he was in his early 30s, had no symptoms and no known risk factors. Prostate cancer is uncommon in men younger than 40, so current guidelines generally would not have recommended screening in his case.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Prostate cancer screening is intended for men who do not have symptoms. Men who develop symptoms — including changes in urination, blood in the urine or semen, or persistent back or hip pain — should see a doctor promptly for evaluation, experts advise.

Smith noted that there is no guaranteed way to prevent prostate cancer, as its biggest risk factors — age, race and family history — cannot be changed.

As with many cancers, however, research suggests that maintaining a healthy lifestyle may help lower the risk. That includes eating a healthy diet, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising regularly, avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol consumption.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"These are behaviors that not only reduce the risk of cancer, but also cardiovascular disease and diabetes," Smith said. "Some studies have suggested that staying sexually active can lower risk, but results are mixed."

"Regular PSA testing can reduce the risk associated with being diagnosed with an advanced prostate cancer."

item.title: Presley Gerber’s final hours at rehab in focus amid cause of death questions
item.description: Presley Gerber's final hours draws questions. Police are investigating the 27-year-old model's death as a suspected overdose.
item.content:encoded:
Presley Gerber died Sunday, Sept. 20 – one day after entering the Resolutions Living rehabilitation facility in Santa Monica, Calif. He was 27.

Based off Wilshire Boulevard in an affluent Southern California community, the center is described as a co-ed home which "provides the structure" for residents on their journey to recovery from mental health, addiction, and co-occurring disorders through intensive outpatient programs of their choosing.

While it remained unclear why Cindy Crawford's son entered the center or what treatment he was receiving, wrongful death and personal injury attorney John J. Perlstein warned against jumping to conclusions of liability as the investigation continued into Gerber's death.

PRESLEY GERBER'S DEATH BEING INVESTIGATED AS 'A SUSPECTED OVERDOSE': POLICE

"I just don't assume what the cause of death is or that the facility failed them or the family ... don't think the family wasn't doing everything they had to do," Perlstein told Fox News Digital.

"It seems like, you know, in these situations the families do so much for the sick person, the person who was addicted."

He added, "By all accounts, they were a very loving, good family, and it's just real sad circumstance. It certainly caught a lot of people's attention. I'll tell you that much."

Gerber, the only son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, died while staying at the rehabilitation facility, according to records from the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner.

KID ROCK CALLS PRESLEY GERBER’S DEATH A ‘TRAGEDY’ AS EX-GIRLFRIEND SAYS HE ‘DESERVED MORE TIME’

The treatment center's website says it draws "on our years of experience in addiction and mental health support," with "experienced staff has supported people with a wide variety of needs, from substance abuse and mental health, to trauma and eating disorders."

Gerber reportedly checked into the facility on Saturday night and died Sunday morning. Representatives for Resolutions Living did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Nicholas Kardaris, Ph.D., CEO and chief clinical officer of the New York Center for Living in Manhattan and a clinical professor at Stony Brook Medicine’s School of Social Welfare, cautioned against drawing conclusions from the fact that he died at a rehabilitation facility.

CINDY CRAWFORD’S SON PRESLEY GERBER SAID HE WAS ‘TERRIFIED’ IN RAW ADDICTION POST MONTHS BEFORE DEATH AT 27

As Gerber’s official cause of death has not yet been released, Kardaris — who has not treated Presley Gerber and is not connected to the case — noted that possible explanations could include an acute medical or cardiac event, an undiagnosed condition or a medication-related complication.

People in residential treatment facilities may have complex medical histories, and some conditions may not be immediately apparent when someone enters a program.

"Younger people can sometimes die suddenly, and we don’t know whether they had an underlying medical issue," Kardaris said.

"It’s not impossible to have a medication-related event, particularly if someone has an underlying heart disorder," he continued. "Certain medications can trigger a cardiac episode."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

He added, "People are in rehab because they’re struggling with addiction. It doesn’t mean they’re cured of their addiction."

Another potential risk during rehab is withdrawal itself, which can range from uncomfortable to life-threatening depending on the substance involved and the person’s level of physical dependence, according to Kardaris.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"People can die from withdrawal, but the substances that are most dangerous to withdraw [from] without proper medical supervision are benzodiazepines, such as Valium or Xanax, and alcohol," he said.

The deputy medical examiner (DME) told Fox News Digital that "the investigation is still ongoing and there is limited information available," and his cause of death has not yet been released.

The DME is in "the early stages of investigating the death of 27-year-old model Presley Gerber and limited information is currently available," according to a statement from the department.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"A deputy medical examiner performed an examination today and the cause and manner of death have been deferred, which means additional testing and/or studies were requested in order to make a determination."

They added, "Due to the ongoing death investigation, the DME cannot disclose what testing and/or studies were requested. Deferred cases can take a few months before a cause of death is determined."

Santa Monica Police Department officials are investigating the death as "a suspected overdose," according to a release from the department.

Officers responded to a report of a possible overdose at approximately 9:35 a.m., Sunday, Sept. 20. Upon arrival, officers located an adult male who was deceased.

At this time, there is no indication of foul play, and Gerber's case remains open. The facility has not been accused of wrongdoing.

A representative for the family told Fox News Digital, "The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time."

Fox News Digital's Melissa Rudy contributed to this report.

item.title: Ambassador Jeff Bartos: UN must abandon anti-American, anti-Western legacy of Durban Conference
item.description: From Fidel Castro's denunciations to the origins of the BDS movement, the U.N.'s Durban conference codified radical anti-Western hatred 25 years ago.
item.content:encoded:

Two hundred and fifty years ago, our founders declared that our unalienable rights did not come from kings, emperors or any earthly government — least of all unelected globalist bureaucrats. They were inherent in man, endowed by God.

Because of the Durban conference, extremist ideologues who had long festered at the fringes of the international system were pulled under one tent, handed credentials and microphones and given the imprimatur of the United Nations.

The United Nations lost something too: credibility. Every time it returns to Durban, it poisons its own brand — and helps fuel the same conflicts it should be fighting to end.
