President Trump has made clear: America will not apologize for being America — or perpetuate a system that teaches others to hate us for our success.

The world has had 25 years to see where the Durban conference’s ideology leads. We must reject its poison of grievance politics and anti-Western hatred. It’s time to burn and bury the Durban conference’s legacy of Third-Worldism and hostility toward Western civilization. Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, the United States will continue to speak out against this evil ideological project in the U.N. system or wherever it appears around the world.

Instead, we welcome allies, partners and friends: Join the United States in embracing pride in our past and confidence in our future — and rejecting the politics of shame, self-hatred and decline.

item.title: Darren Rovell details how bad financial advice cost NBA legend Kobe Bryant an easy $23M payday

"You know, once a year you interview me on business. I think you're one of the smartest guys. I love business too, haven't done anything, and would love to figure out if there's some business thing we can get into together. Can I have your number?"

"3 a.m., 2 a.m., every time. Every time I responded, even though he was in L.A., there was the dot, dot, dot back. He's awake... same cycling brain, same everything," Rovell shared.

item.content:encoded:
Before Jacob Bridgeman joined Russell Henley, Sam Burns and Scottie Scheffler on the 2026 U.S. Presidents Cup team, he already had a connection with them.

A shared Christian faith.

"I think probably my relationships with Russell, Sam, [and] Scottie have all kind of come from our faith, us being in this community together and all sharing the same background and the same beliefs," Bridgeman told OutKick on Tuesday.

Now, as the Americans prepare to compete at Medinah Country Club, several players say those shared beliefs have helped them grow closer. They also told OutKick what their faith means when golf becomes frustrating and bad shots start to feel a little too important.

"It gives me a lot of freedom to go out and compete and know that no matter what happens, my identity is not in the result of the match, the result of the Presidents Cup," Burns said. "It's in my faith and being a believer in Jesus."

SAM BURNS IS ONE OF AMERICA'S BEST GOLFERS, BUT FAITH, FAMILY AND THE USA MATTER MORE TO HIM THAN GOLF

U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker said the team's closeness extends beyond shared religious beliefs, but he has seen faith strengthen relationships among some of his players.

"It's definitely helped bond those guys for sure," Snedeker said. "They spend a lot of time together. They have Bible studies together on Tour."

"Anything these guys do off the golf course to bring them together, I'm all for it," he continued. "These guys are great human beings."

Cameron Young sees a connection, too.

"I wouldn't say it's a huge topic, but I think just when you get a group of people that generally believe in the same underlying principles you're going to have some level of connection or bond with them," Young said.

Henley said there are typically Bible studies on Tuesday nights during Tour events. He also described working through a book with someone from College Golf Fellowship, a Christian ministry serving golfers and coaches, and joining a weekly conference call.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"So that's my community I guess when I'm on the road," Henley said.

Henley and Burns said Tuesday that the busy schedule had not yet allowed for a formal Bible study among the players this week.

For Bridgeman, those friendships also helped him deal with the pressure he put on himself when he first got on Tour. Older players helped him understand that his value isn't contingent on playing good golf.

"I think over the last few years, I've grown a lot in my understanding that I'm not measured by the number that I shoot," Bridgeman said. "Even though I shoot a 65, I'm not any better of a person than the day when I shoot a 75."

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

But what does relying on faith actually look like when a round isn't going well?

OutKick put that question to Henley, who said he thinks about the day when he'll be too old to play at this level. His Christian beliefs give him a reason to look beyond his golf career.

"I don't know that I necessarily rely on my faith to play better, but I think knowing that I'm going to have a place in heaven because of what I believe and what Jesus has done for me, not anything I've done, because of what he's done, definitely gives me peace," Henley said.

"That doesn't mean I don't get nervous and frustrated and struggle with anger, but I know what I think the truth is and what I believe to be true," he said. "I think just knowing that is an encouragement."

Asked in an August OutKick interview whether golf had ever tested his faith, Burns answered, "Every day."

"You can hit really good shots and end up in bad places, or bad shots end up in good places," Burns told OutKick last month. "Sometimes it seems silly, but ultimately it's a game that teaches you a lot about life and definitely can make you realize what's most important."

Young echoed that sentiment on Tuesday, noting that while he has dedicated a large part of his life to becoming one of the best golfers in the world and cares deeply about how he plays, he tries to keep golf in perspective.

"Just from a competitive standpoint I really care about doing well," Young said. "[Golf is] not the most important thing in the world, there's things far more important, but at the same time it's my job and it's something that I've dedicated a large portion of my life to."

For Young, having a healthy family puts the frustration of a bad round of golf in perspective.

"When you don't play well, it's just not the end of the world," he said.

"My children are healthy, my family's healthy, that's where things are hard. Golf is not hard in that sense."

item.title: Ex-Democrat shares abortion pill experience that left her 'hemorrhaging in the bath'
item.description: Haile McAnally says she nearly bled to death after taking abortion pills and is now heading to Capitol Hill to curb mail-order mifepristone.
item.content:encoded:
Nebraska resident Haile McAnally believes it was "divine intervention" that saved her from bleeding to death in her own bathroom shortly after high school.

She told Fox News Digital that abortion medication, in the form of pills, was to blame for her having "hemorrhaged in the bath," and that she is now focused on sparing other women the same possible fate.

"Planned Parenthood told us that this is what is women empowerment. This is what women do when they can't handle it. They take this route, and they don't acknowledge the pain it causes," McAnally said. 

"The same pills I took under direction of medical professionals, they can be shipped anywhere at any time," she continued. "I can't imagine being a young woman in college and maybe finding herself in this position, ordering these pills online, not knowing what kind of maybe pre-medical condition she has, and she finds herself in the same position."

FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS

McAnally said the experience is also part of what motivated her to switch parties from a pro-choice "registered Democrat" to a pro-life Republican.

"I had always been on the left because I thought they were the side that was more open to having these conversations, the free-thinkers," she recalled.

McAnally said her questions about how and why her ordeal happened were met with, "You can't talk about it. You can't talk about it because it's not part of our agenda. It's not a part of our platform to talk about any complications this may have."

"I noticed the more I asked questions, the people on the right were more willing to talk about it, which, in the pro-life space, I thought I was gonna be condemned. I thought it was gonna like, 'You're gonna go to hell. This is horrible. You're a murderer.' These things that you always hear from the left that the right is gonna call you," she said.

And I was like, 'I'm gonna talk about it and see what happens.' And the right was so forgiving and so loving and really embraced my story and really said, 'This is horrible, I'm glad you seek forgiveness and counsel for this.'"

McAnally told Fox News Digital that it had always been her dream to become a mother. When she got pregnant by her boyfriend, however, she said he had a very different response.

"He asked me what I was gonna do about it and hung up the phone, and I haven't talked to him since," she said.

She recalled being fearful of going through the experience alone and turning to pro-choice groups for guidance.

"I remember seeing the pink signs everywhere and the marketing that says ... the sisterhood will take care of you," she said. "And as someone in that position where you're scared, and you are looking for answers somewhere, and you don't wanna be alone and being so young at the time, that was a very enticing message."

PLANNED PARENTHOOD ACROSS MIDWEST AT RISK DUE TO LACK OF FEDERAL FUNDS AFTER 3 FACILITIES CLOSE IN MICHIGAN

McAnally described the clinic as being "cold," "dark," and smelling of rubbing alcohol.

"They took my money, and they sent me back to this room where ... this doctor was going to walk me through everything that was going to happen that day. That's the consent kind of happened, in that room, and he didn't know me from Adam. He really didn't ask about my background and anything medical that's ever happened," she recalled.

ABORTION PILL FIGHT HEADS TO SUPREME COURT AS MANUFACTURER WARNS OF ‘CHAOS’ AFTER RULING

But as an "emotional and scared" young woman, McAnally said she signed the consent forms and was given one abortion pill and told to take a second one at home. She said medical staff warned her it would feel like "a more intense period," recommending a heating pad and tea for comfort.

"I followed that protocol, went home, took the second pill, and I found myself on the toilet in the bathroom where bleeding occurred, which was exactly what they said. But after about two hours, I was still bleeding out. And I started feeling really weak. I knew that what was happening was not right, but I couldn't really comprehend what was going on," McAnally said.

I CHOSE ABORTION, THEN CHANGED MY MIND — CALIFORNIA WANTS THAT CHOICE GONE

She said she dragged herself into the bathtub before realizing her condition had quickly become serious — but that her phone was out of reach.

"I just laid there and thought that was the moment that everything was over, and, partially, I felt like it was punishment for me making that decision," she said. "But at the end of the day, I remember waking up, and I was in the hospital and my friend had come home, and she had realized that I was laying in the bathtub unconscious at the time, and she called 911, and I had a blood transfusion done."

McAnally said she now feels like it's her duty to warn other women of the potential dangers of unfettered access to mifepristone.

That's why she and several other women allied with anti-abortion group Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America are heading to Capitol Hill on Thursday to meet with lawmakers and staffers. Their plea: curb access to mail-order abortion pills.

"Women who’ve suffered the devastating effects of abortion drugs who are clear-eyed about the lies of the Big Abortion industry are the most effective advocates," said SBA Pro-Life America President Marjorie Dannenfelser. "Their lives are forever changed, but they’re standing strong and having a powerful impact on Capitol Hill and beyond."

A study in JAMA Internal Medicine observed that 0.6% of women who get mail-order abortion pills experience medical emergencies that leave them hospitalized. A conflicting study by the Ethics and Public Policy Center said one in 10 women have a "serious adverse event."

It's a testament to the volatile, often emotional politics that have consumed the abortion debate in the wake of the Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade.

Fox News Digital reached out to Planned Parenthood for comment.

item.title: Trump-backed Iowa US Senate hopeful says Iran war must 'be brought to a successful and immediate end'
item.description: Trump-backed U.S. Senate candidate U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson asserted that the Iran "war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end."
item.content:encoded:
As Americans endure elevated fuel costs with the midterm elections on the horizon, Rep. Ashley Hinson — a Republican running for U.S. Senate in Iowa — asserted in a post on X that the Iran war should "be brought to a successful and immediate end."

"Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices," Hinson said in the Monday post on X.

"That includes suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports, unleashing E-15 everywhere we can, reinstating the $1/gallon biodiesel tax credit, and creating a diesel relief program to help our farmers and truckers being crushed by the high costs," she continued.

FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR

"While doing this, we should also ensure our highway trust fund is replenished, so that Iowans don’t suffer from crumbling roads and bridges while relief comes our way now. These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end," Hinson wrote.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House on Wednesday.

Hinson announced a U.S. Senate bid last year on the same day that Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, announced that she would not run for re-election. President Donald Trump then endorsed Hinson for the Senate seat days later.

TRUMP-BACKED SENATE CANDIDATE SAYS 'GROCERIES COST TOO MUCH,' CALLS FOR IRAN WAR TO 'END QUICKLY'

Hinson is running against Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, who is backed by former President Barack Obama.

The congresswoman has served in the U.S. House of Representatives since early 2021.

SEVEN-FIGURE BLITZ AS GOP EMBRACES PUSH TO COMPETE WITH CHINA IN BOOMING NEW TECH SPACE

During an address to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said, "But I have a big decision to make. Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before ... Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?"

item.title: China’s Xi set to arrive in Washington for high-stakes Trump summit as AI supremacy battle looms large
item.description: China's President Xi Jinping arrives for a tense White House summit with Trump covering AI, tariffs, rare earth minerals and fentanyl exports.
item.content:encoded:
China's President Xi Jinping is set to arrive on U.S. soil later Wednesday for what is expected to be a tense showdown between President Donald Trump and the communist leader.

A red carpet rollout is planned for when Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrive at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday evening, replete with an arrival ceremony for the man who has found himself at odds with Trump on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and intellectual property theft, trade practices, rare-earth minerals to the communist country's support for Iran during America's military conflict there. Xi hasn't visited the nation's capital in more than a decade.

AI will be a major topic of discussion during the two-day summit, which officially begins Thursday morning and ends Friday evening, according to a senior administration official. Thursday will begin with a prestigious State Arrival Ceremony, including 479 military personnel from all branches on the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House.

XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT

According to the official, a wide-ranging deal on possible tariff reductions on non-strategic goods is an expected topic of discussion, who also said the nation's leaders will discuss rare-earth exports and possible export controls. Trump is also expected to press China to do more to curb fentanyl precursor chemical exports.

Trump is also likely to press for the release of an American who has been wrongfully detained in China, Gulshan Abbas, who has languished in a Chinese prison for eight years. The country accused her of "participating in a terrorist organization" after her sister spoke out about China's genocide of Uyghurs, according to Forbes. House Speaker Mike Johnson and other Republicans have expressed confidence that Trump will push for her release.

EXCLUSIVE: FENTANYL DEATHS PLUNGE 22% AS TRUMP WHITE HOUSE TOUTS CRACKDOWN ON DEADLY DRUG CRISIS

First lady Melania Trump is expected to accompany Peng to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, "to explore works spanning centuries of artistic achievement and Sino-American cultural exchange."

The day will end with an elaborate state dinner with high-profile guests, including many from the tech world.

Those guests will include Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, SpaceX founder and former Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) head Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser and Apple Board of Directors Chairman Tim Cook.

Trump boasted about American AI supremacy over China during an address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York Tuesday, using his newly-minted term for the technology, "superintelligence."

TRUMP'S AI RACE WITH CHINA COULD BECOME THE BIGGEST MISTAKE OF OUR TIME

"Every major new technology brings challenges, and superintelligence is no exception," said Trump. "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. That's the group that wins. And we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else. And we're going to keep it that way."

Trump traveled to Beijing in May where he met with Xi, and the two sides agreed to a "constructive" trade truce, pausing a tit-for-tat tariff battle, but only for non-strategic goods. That deal has tentatively held, but during that visit, China also agreed to purchase billions more in American agricultural products like soybeans, and 200 Boeing aircraft. Boeing confirmed the order.

The 47th president said at the time that he struck "fantastic trade deals" that were "great for both countries."

item.title: Bringing this popular drink to a job interview could hurt your chances, experts warn
item.description: An etiquette expert warns that bringing iced coffee or other beverages to a job interview signals casualness and says the professionalism rule applies to all ages.
item.content:encoded:
A cup of coffee might be a daily ritual for most Americans, but some career and etiquette experts say bringing one into a job interview could hurt your chances of getting hired.

A viral debate has erupted over whether an iced coffee sends the wrong message to hiring managers or if it's simply part of a busy day.

Caitlin Wehniainen, a Florida-based corporate recruiter with 16 years of experience recruiting for Fortune 500 companies, sparked the conversation with a video in which she called out Gen Z job candidates for going to interviews with a coffee in hand.

CAN YOU BRING A BIRTHDAY CAKE TO A RESTAURANT? VIRAL PIZZERIA DISPUTE REVEALS THE RULES

"When you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte, it is perceived — from my opinion and a hiring standpoint — that this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day," she said in a recent TikTok video that has amassed more than 17,000 likes and 5,000 comments. 

"It looks like you went to Target, went to Starbucks, and now you're stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing."

It looks "a little too casual," Wehniainen added. "Save that for well before the interview or after the interview. Go and get one. But don’t like waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee. It just looks like you didn’t have time to finish your coffee beforehand."

Social media users flooded the comment section, with many agreeing that it is "diabolical" to bring a wet cup dripping with condensation and rattling with ice into the room.

WHY RESTAURANT SERVERS CLEAR YOUR PLATE BEFORE EVERYONE FINISHES EATING

"That generation has lost the art of professionalism," one TikToker commented.

The viral coffee debate joins a growing list of workplace faux pas involving Gen Z, including bringing parents to sit in on interviews, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

But others stood up for candidates getting their caffeine fix during an interview.

GEN Z TURNS ON CLASSIC SNACKS, FORCING MAJOR GROCERY SHAKE-UP: 'THEY DON'T TRUST THEM'

"An interview IS just a stop in my day," one woman said on TikTok. "It's not my whole day."

"Are you expecting my whole day to revolve around a 30 min meeting," someone else said.

A man who said he was also a recruiter offered another point of view: "If you can show up early or on time with the iced coffee you're already showing good time management."

COMMUNAL DINING MAKES GEN Z COMEBACK, BUT OLDER GUESTS PUSH BACK ON 'CHAOTIC' TREND

Others pointed to the already challenging job market.

"If showing up with a beverage like a coffee is an issue … that's not a company that I want to work for," someone commented on TikTok.

Others said it's more nuanced. One TikToker noted that, since Wehniainen recruits for Fortune 500 companies, interviews and candidates tend to be more "buttoned up," but that won't be the case everywhere.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Diane Gottsman, a national etiquette expert and the owner of the Protocol School of Texas, said it's therefore best to "err on the side of caution."

"Perception is everything," Gottsman told Fox News Digital. "What one person may think is fine, another person may not."

"I think bringing in that cup of iced coffee signals both a distraction, a level of comfort and casualness that may not be there," she said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"We're not pointing the finger only at a certain generation," Gottsman added, noting that workers of all ages make similar etiquette mistakes.

Beyond coffee, Gottsman said candidates should avoid other distractions or unprofessional impressions by putting away their phones, skipping overpowering fragrances, removing sunglasses from the tops of their heads and avoiding chewing gum.

As distracting as an iced latte can be during an in-person job interview, there's another item that can irk hiring managers: the cellphone.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"One job candidate not only placed her cellphone face up on the conference room table during our interview, she also repeatedly leaned over to read incoming texts and even began texting as well while I was speaking to her," said one New York-based manager.

The interview ended early. The candidate was not hired.

If an interviewer offers coffee or water, Gottsman said, it's perfectly acceptable to accept — but don't ask for more than what was offered. And if candidates need a drink of water from a bottle tucked away in a bag, she recommends politely asking before taking a sip.

Gottsman also noted that interviews are a two-way street. While employers are evaluating candidates, applicants should also be deciding whether a company's culture and expectations are the right fit for them.

She and Wehniainen agree that there is a time and place for everything.

"After your job interview, why not treat yourself to your favorite iced coffee drink as a treat for a job well done?" Gottsman added.
